chunks.passage: Neural Networks

chunks.title: The Artificial Neuron
chunks.passage:
The Artificial Neuron
An artificial neuron is a small calculation, loosely inspired by biological neurons.
Receive inputs: numbers from the data or an earlier layer.
Multiply each input by its weight, then add the results.
Add a bias: a learned offset.
Apply an activation function and pass the output onward.
One neuron makes one feature. Connecting many neurons lets the model combine features.

One neuron, one decision: take inputs, multiply by weights, output a score. Score > 0.5 → Yes. Score < 0.5 → No. That’s classification. One neuron isn’t smart: but millions together can recognize faces, translate languages, and write code.

chunks.title: The Neuron as a Formula
chunks.passage:
The Neuron as a Formula
output = activation(weight₁ × input₁ + weight₂ × input₂ + bias)
A weight controls how an input changes this neuron’s calculation. It can be positive, negative, or near zero.
The bias shifts the calculation, like the intercept in a regression.
The activation bends the response. The next layer receives this result.
In the previous demo, change just one weight. Then change just the bias. Which part of the formula moved?

chunks.title: Why Nonlinearity Matters
chunks.passage:
Why Nonlinearity Matters
Move the input across zero. Compare a straight response with a response that bends.
Stacking only linear layers still gives a linear function. Nonlinear activations let layers combine into curved decision boundaries.

chunks.title: Inspired by the Brain
chunks.passage:
Inspired by the Brain
Biological neuron
Biological: receives and sends electrochemical signals.
Artificial neuron
Artificial: combines numbers with weights, bias, and an activation.
The connection is an inspiration. This simplified mathematical model does not reproduce all the ways a brain learns.

chunks.title: A Brain and a Neural Network
chunks.passage:
A Brain and a Neural Network
Biological brain
Artificial neural network
[Image description] A stylized brain filled with branching biological neurons beside a matching brain-shaped artificial network, with blue input nodes, four purple hidden layers of varying heights, teal output nodes, and a left-to-right signal arrow.
The shared idea: many connected units passing signals.
Biological neurons inspire the idea. Artificial neurons are simplified calculations.

chunks.title: One Neuron → A Network
chunks.passage:
One Neuron → A Network
Our small network reads three pixel values and predicts stripe or solid. Trace its connections.
Hidden just means between input and output. Those neurons produce intermediate numbers, not answers we label by hand.

chunks.title: How a Neural Network Learns
chunks.passage:
How a Neural Network Learns
Imagine a row of adjustable dials. Together, their settings determine the prediction.
Predict: pass an example through the network with the current settings.
Measure loss: compare the prediction with its training target.
Backpropagate: calculate how a small change to each setting would change loss.
Update: use those gradients to adjust the weights and biases.
Repeat: use many examples, then check held-out examples.
Backpropagation measures sensitivity. The optimizer uses that information to move the dials.

chunks.title: The Training Loop
chunks.passage:
The Training Loop
Step through one complete training update. Watch when the parameters actually change.
The forward pass, loss, and backward pass use the current weights. Only the update step changes them.

chunks.title: What’s Actually Being Adjusted?
chunks.passage:
What’s Actually Being Adjusted?
Choose a connection and move its weight. The input stays fixed; the prediction changes.
This network has 20 connection weights + 6 biases = 26 learned parameters. Inputs are data; neuron outputs are calculated values.

chunks.title: Parameters vs Hyperparameters
chunks.passage:
Parameters vs Hyperparameters
[Image description] Parameters are dials inside the network: training changes a connection weight from 0.20 to 0.24 and a neuron bias from 0.10 to 0.12. Hyperparameters are the setup controls we choose: layers and neurons, learning rate, and training duration. The number changes are illustrative.
The model learns parameters
Connection weights.
Neuron biases.
The 26 numbers in our small network.
We choose hyperparameters
Number of layers and neurons.
Activation function.
Learning rate and training duration.
Check: which one do we choose for the training process?

chunks.title: Batches Make Training Practical
chunks.passage:
Batches Make Training Practical
A mini-batch is a small group of training examples used for one update. Here, the batch is four pictures.
[Image description] One mini-batch contains four labeled pictures: two stripes and two solid colors. All four pass through the same neural network. Four losses provide gradients that are averaged, followed by one update to the shared network. Then training takes the next batch.
1. Predict and comparePredict for each picture and measure its loss against its label.
2. Combine the feedbackBackpropagation gives gradients for each example. Average those gradients.
3. Update onceApply one update to the shared weights and biases. Then take the next batch.
Examples can pull a parameter in opposite directions. The batch update follows their average, not the last example alone.

chunks.title: Epochs Revisit the Dataset
chunks.passage:
Epochs Revisit the Dataset
One epoch is one full pass through the training data.
[Image description] Two epochs through the same 100 training examples. Each row contains ten batches of ten examples, with one parameter update per batch. Epoch 2 keeps the learned weights from epoch 1, reaching twenty updates in total.
Batch size 10 with 100 examples means 10 updates per epoch.
At the next epoch, the model sees the examples again with new parameter values.
More epochs can reduce training loss while making performance on new examples worse.
Return to the circle experiment. Compare training loss and held-out loss after more epochs. Did both improve?
Tip
Use a validation set to choose when to stop. Keep a separate test set for the final evaluation.

chunks.title: CNNs at a Glance
chunks.passage:
CNNs at a Glance
A convolutional neural network reuses small filters across an image.
The same filter weights are used at every position. Training learns the filters; sliding a trained filter is part of the forward pass. Pac-Man’s CNN uses this idea to process the game screen.

chunks.title: Why GPUs Help Train Networks
chunks.passage:
Why GPUs Help Train Networks
Training repeats many similar calculations across neurons and examples.
[Image description] A GPU rack processes three batches in parallel with the same weight matrix. A zoom shows inputs [1, 2] multiplied by weights [[0.20, -0.40], [0.70, 0.10]] to produce layer scores [1.60, -0.20]. Loss and gradients guide an optimizer update, changing the weights to [[0.18, -0.37], [0.66, 0.12]] before the next batches.
A layer can be calculated as a matrix multiplication, followed by bias and activation.
Many of those calculations can run at the same time.
GPUs provide hardware for doing large groups of numerical operations in parallel.
The small network we just trained uses the same basic learning loop. A larger network needs more memory, computation, and data.

chunks.title: Biocomputing: Living Neurons Play Doom
chunks.passage:
Biocomputing: Living Neurons Play Doom
[Image description] News headline: Human brain cells on a chip learned to play Doom in a week, with an illustration of neurons and a Cortical Labs device.
Watch the Cortical Labs demonstration ↗
[Image description] AI-generated conceptual image of a small piece of brain tissue resting on a microchip with gold electrical contacts.
Biocomputing connects living neurons to software. The Doom demonstration combines cells on a chip with digital reinforcement learning.
Remember Pac-Man? Reward feedback helps update the network's predictions of future return.
The brain has a related teaching signal: dopamine can track whether a reward was better or worse than expected.
The connection is learning from prediction errors. Artificial networks minimize a defined loss; the brain's biological learning rules are different.
Sources: Doom experiment and code · Schultz, Dayan & Montague, 1997

chunks.title: Autocomplete: Choosing Among Words
chunks.passage:
Autocomplete: Choosing Among Words
A familiar example from the 2000s and 2010s: Google Search autocomplete.
[Image description] Google autocomplete for 'why is uc berkeley so', suggesting prestigious, hard to get into, expensive, liberal, good, and other completions.
Google Suggest launched in 2004; it reached Google.com in 2008. Screenshot: today’s interface.
Words as categories. A traditional encoding gives each word its own position in a fixed vocabulary.
prestigious
expensive
good
Next-word prediction becomes multiclass classification: assign a probability to each possible next word.
Google’s autocomplete illustrates the experience: rank likely query completions using search patterns and other signals.
These numbers identify words. How could numbers also capture their meaning?

chunks.title: Teaching Machines to Read
chunks.passage: Teaching Machines to Read

chunks.title: Why Language?
chunks.passage:
Why Language?
So far, every model we’ve seen works with numbers: house prices, pixel values, game screens.
But the biggest AI breakthroughs came from teaching machines to read text
Why? The internet is mostly text. Trillions of words, freely available
If you can teach a machine to read, you can train it on the entire internet
Note
This is exactly what happened. The shift from images to language is what gave us ChatGPT, Claude, and every modern AI assistant.

chunks.title: The Problem: Words Aren’t Numbers
chunks.passage:
The Problem: Words Aren’t Numbers
How do you feed words into a neural network that only understands numbers?
An embedding is a learned vector (a list of numbers) that represents a word or token. Training adjusts these numbers to help the model make predictions.
[Image description] Cat and dog embeddings compared along the same dimensions: wildness, size, and furriness. Their first two dimensions are also shown as nearby points.
Warning
Both words use the same dimensions, in the same order. These values and labels are simplified examples; real dimensions are learned and blend many concepts. Words used in similar contexts tend to have similar embeddings.

chunks.title: Words as Points in Space
chunks.passage:
Words as Points in Space
Word2Vec (2013) learned that words in similar contexts get similar vectors.
“The ___ sat on the mat” → cat, dog, child all fit → similar vectors.
Words with similar meanings cluster together. Relationships like gender, royalty, and age become directions you can navigate with math.
Important
king - man + woman ≈ queen
The model learned gender as a direction in vector space, without anyone teaching it!

chunks.title: Distance Reflects Meaning
chunks.passage:
Distance Reflects Meaning
An embedding represents a word as a vector. Nearby vectors can capture related meanings.
“Dog” and “puppy” have related meanings, so their vectors are close together.
“Dog” and “airplane” have less in common, so their vectors are farther apart.
The dashed lines measure distance between vectors. A smaller distance represents greater similarity in this example.
[Image description] Word embedding vectors from a shared origin: dog=[4,2], puppy=[3.5,3], airplane=[0.5,3]. Dashed links show Euclidean distances from dog: 1.12 to puppy, similar meaning; 3.64 to airplane, different meaning.
Illustrative 2D embeddings. Distances calculated from the coordinates shown.
Tip
Meaning becomes something we can compare with math: “dog” is closer to “puppy” than to “airplane.”

chunks.title: Explore Word Embeddings in 3D
chunks.passage:
Explore Word Embeddings in 3D
Tip
Word2Vec 10K loads automatically. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, and search for “king” to see nearby words. Try toggling between PCA and t-SNE projections.

chunks.title: Context Determines Meaning
chunks.passage:
Context Determines Meaning
One vector per word has a ceiling: “bank” in a finance memo and “bank” in a river report should not mean the same thing.
Word2Vec gives both banks the same point in space: a learned representation based on the contexts in its training corpus. Modern models instead create contextual representations: the vector for “bank” is adjusted, on the fly, by the words around it. The mechanism that does that adjusting is attention: coming right up.

chunks.title: Context Moves “Bank” in Embedding Space
chunks.passage:
Context Moves “Bank” in Embedding Space
[Image description] Three-dimensional embedding space with a base bank vector in orange. Adding river as context shifts it to a blue river bank vector near river. Adding money as context shifts it to a teal money bank vector near the base bank vector and money. Solid arrows are embedding vectors from a common origin; dashed arrows show changes from added context.
Illustrative 3D positions. + means adding context, not exact vector addition.

chunks.title: How Words Become Tokens
chunks.passage:
How Words Become Tokens
A tokenizer breaks text into pieces called tokens. BPE (byte-pair encoding) learns which pieces to combine.
[Image description] Illustrative tokenization of unbelievable. Individual letters combine into un, bel, iev, able, then into three tokens: un, believ, able. Each token has an ID that selects a learned embedding vector.
Illustrative split, IDs, and vectors. Each model uses its own fixed tokenizer.
One word, three tokens: each takes context space and can contribute to API cost.

chunks.title: Talking in Tokens
chunks.passage:
Talking in Tokens
[Image description] A cartoon caveman proudly uses a stone computer displaying ME WANT FOOD. Meme caption: WHY USE MANY WORD, WHEN FEW TOKEN DO TRICK?
Tokenization splits text into pieces and preserves the original wording.

chunks.title: Sequences & Attention
chunks.passage: Sequences & Attention

chunks.title: The Problem with Order
chunks.passage:
The Problem with Order
“Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” use the same words but mean different things.
A representation that only counts words loses their order.
A network can use order if the input and architecture preserve it.
Sequence models are designed to work with positions and context.
The design question is: how should information at one position influence another?

chunks.title: RNNs: Adding Memory
chunks.passage:
RNNs: Adding Memory
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) process sequences one step at a time, passing a “memory” forward to the next step: a running state that summarizes everything read so far.
The fading arrows illustrate a possible difficulty with long-range information, not a fixed five-word memory limit. Each recurrent step depends on the previous state.

chunks.title: The Bottleneck Problem
chunks.passage:
The Bottleneck Problem
A recurrent network carries a fixed-size state from one position to the next.
[Image description] Input tokens enter repeated RNN steps one at a time. Each step combines its token with the previous hidden state and produces a new summary in numbers. Hidden states h0, h1, h2, and ht keep the same size even across many more tokens, making earlier details harder to preserve. A green-to-red arrow runs to the right of the earlier-details caption.
That state must retain useful details from earlier positions.
Long-range relationships can be difficult to learn and preserve.
The dependence on the previous state limits parallel processing across positions.
Attention offers a more direct route between positions. It does not need to pass every detail through a single running state.

chunks.title: “Attention Is All You Need” (2017)
chunks.passage:
“Attention Is All You Need” (2017)
In 2017, Google researchers published arguably the most important AI paper of the decade. The solution to RNNs forgetting and being slow? Don’t process words one at a time at all.
They introduced the Transformer: built entirely on a mechanism called attention, with no recurrence. Every major AI model today: GPT, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA: is a transformer.

chunks.title: Attention Changes the Question
chunks.passage:
Attention Changes the Question
Attention combines information from the token positions available to the current position.
A recurrent network passes a state forward through the sequence.
Attention can connect directly to earlier positions within the context window.
In a GPT-style model, a causal mask blocks future tokens.
Training can process many positions in parallel while respecting that mask. Generating new text still proceeds one token at a time.

chunks.title: Attention: Which Tokens Can It Use?
chunks.passage:
Attention: Which Tokens Can It Use?
Select a position. Which tokens is it allowed to use to predict the next token?
In a GPT-style model, a position can attend to itself and earlier positions. Future positions are masked out. Allowed does not mean equally useful.

chunks.title: Attention Can Connect Distant Words
chunks.passage:
Attention Can Connect Distant Words
[Image description] The full book page contains 31 highlighted references and 29 backward connections. Purple links Mr Dursley with he and his; teal links the Dursleys with they and their; amber links Mrs Dursley with she and her. Prominent curves connect the final paragraph directly to earlier names. This is an illustration, not measured attention weights.
A word can draw on useful context many sentences earlier.
Mr Dursley · he · his
The Dursleys · they · their
Mrs Dursley · she · her
The last “he” can still connect to the first “Mr Dursley”.
The long curves show direct connections across paragraphs.
Attention can reach back within the context window.
Arrows point to earlier context. Illustrative connections, not measured attention weights. Real models use tokens.

chunks.title: Why This Matters: Same Word, Different Meaning
chunks.passage:
Why This Matters: Same Word, Different Meaning
“Mole” can refer to an animal, a chemistry unit, or a skin mark.
The token’s starting embedding is shared. Its representation changes as the network combines it with the available context.

chunks.title: Attention Updates Meaning
chunks.passage:
Attention Updates Meaning
After attention, the embedding for “mole” has been pulled toward the right meaning by its context:
“American shrew” pulls “mole” toward the animal direction. “Carbon dioxide” pulls it toward the chemistry direction. Same starting point, different ending: that’s what attention does.

chunks.title: How Attention Combines Context
chunks.passage:
How Attention Combines Context
[Image description] The original attention illustration shows information from context flowing into a token's representation.
Find useful context: compare the current token with the tokens it can use.
Set the mix: give more relevant tokens a larger share.
Update meaning: combine their information with the current representation.

chunks.title: Attention Cost Matters
chunks.passage:
Attention Cost Matters
The price of “every word looks at every other word”: the work grows with the square of the length.
1,000 tokens → 1M comparisons. 100,000 tokens → 10 billion. Doubling your document quadruples the compute
This is the engineering and economic constraint behind context windows: the caps on how much text a model can consider at once
It’s why long-context models cost more per request, why providers charge per token, and why “just paste the whole database into the prompt” is not an architecture
Note
When we discuss context windows, token economics, and retrieval in Class 5, this quadratic is the physics underneath every pricing table you’ll see.

chunks.passage:
How a Transformer Processes Text
[Image description] Six steps in an S-shaped flow: tokenize The cat sat on the; embed tokens with position information; apply repeated attention and neural-network blocks; predict mat 60%, rug 25%, floor 10%, other 5%; sample a random number from 00 to 99, with 73 selecting rug from the 60 to 84 range; append rug to the input and repeat. chunks.title: Generating Text, One Token at a Time
chunks.passage:
Generating Text, One Token at a Time
Each new token becomes part of the next input.
Use the text so far to predict the next token.
Illustrative sequence. Tokens are shown as words and punctuation; real tokens can also be word pieces.

chunks.title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Questions at Once
chunks.passage:
Multi-Head Attention: Several Questions at Once
Multiple heads compute different mixtures in parallel, each with its own learned projections.
[Image description] Comparison of previous sequential models with transformers: the transformer mixes information directly across token positions.
Attention connects information across tokens.
[Image description] Several attention heads, each with its own learned query, key, and value matrices and attention pattern.
Each head learns its own set of matrices.
Heads can capture different relationships, sometimes including syntax or reference.
We choose the number of heads; training learns their parameters.
Heads are not assigned neat human jobs, and attention weights alone do not fully explain a prediction.

chunks.title: Encode, Embed, Decode
chunks.passage:
Encode, Embed, Decode
The decoder builds a context vector, then scores the possible next tokens.
[Image description] Simple whiteboard illustration with two opposing funnel outlines and a vector-space drawing between them. The text The cat sat on the enters the left funnel, labeled Encode context, embeddings plus attention. In the middle, blue vectors for cat, sat, and the final the extend from a shared origin on two axes. The final the vector is highlighted as the context vector and feeds the right funnel, labeled Decode next token, score output vectors. Illustrative choices are mat 70 percent, rug 20 percent, sofa 5 percent, and other tokens 5 percent. A green check selects mat; a return arrow says append mat and repeat.
Decoder layers build the context vector; the output layer scores the next tokens. The funnels show information flow, not literal layer sizes.

chunks.title: Positional Information Preserves Order
chunks.passage:
Positional Information Preserves Order
The same word needs a signal for where it appears, as well as what it means.
[Image description] Two twelve-word sentences use the same words in different orders: After the meeting the manager thanked the analyst for checking the report; After checking the report the analyst thanked the manager for the meeting. Manager appears at position 5 in the first sentence and position 9 in the second. The same word embedding plus different position encodings produces different input representations for attention. Illustrative four-number vectors show the addition explicitly.
RNNs tracked order one step at a time. Attention needs position information supplied explicitly.
Shown here: add a position vector to each embedding before attention mixes the context.

chunks.title: Residual Connections Keep Learning Stable
chunks.passage:
Residual Connections Keep Learning Stable
A detail that made 96-layer networks possible: each block adds its output to its input, rather than replacing it.
Layers refine an existing representation instead of repeatedly rebuilding it from scratch: edit the memo, don’t rewrite it
It also keeps backpropagation healthy: correction signals flow backward through the “shortcut” without fading across dozens of layers (the vanishing gradient problem that plagued early deep networks)
You’ve already seen this: the mole diagram: context is added to the original embedding. That plus sign is a residual connection

chunks.title: Scaling Laws: How Compute Improves Predictions
chunks.passage:
Scaling Laws: How Compute Improves Predictions
When model size and training data grow together, more training compute tends to reduce prediction loss.
[Image description] Model size and training data determine the calculations needed for training, illustrated by a GPU server and clock. A schematic curve shows prediction loss falling as training compute increases, with big early gains and smaller improvements requiring more compute. Model and data should scale together. This is an illustrative trend, not measured results.

chunks.title: Pretraining Learns Broad Statistical Structure
chunks.passage:
Pretraining Learns Broad Statistical Structure
The recipe behind every foundation model:
Take massive text corpora: a filtered slice of the internet, books, code
One task, repeated trillions of times: predict the missing or next token
No labels, no annotators: the text itself is the supervision. Every sentence is a tiny exam with the answer key attached
Result: surprisingly general capabilities: grammar, facts, style, reasoning patterns: from a task nobody would call intelligent
Note
Remember the labeling bottleneck from Class 3: “the biggest cost in ML is labeled data”? Pretraining is the industry-scale workaround: text supplies its own prediction targets if your task is “guess the next token.” Data still requires collection, filtering, and permission to use. That economic unlock, as much as any architecture, is why language became AI’s center of gravity.

chunks.title: Transfer Learning: Don’t Start From Scratch
chunks.passage:
Transfer Learning: Don’t Start From Scratch
Reuse a pretrained network as a starting point, then adapt it to another task.
A pretrained image network can be adapted to a smaller labeled image dataset.
A pretrained language model can be adapted using examples of a specialized task.
Fine-tuning changes parameters; providing context in a prompt does not.
Pretraining can be expensive at large scale. Our tiny classroom model is small enough to train from scratch.

chunks.title: Fine-Tuning and Alignment Shape Behavior
chunks.passage:
Fine-Tuning and Alignment Shape Behavior
A pretrained model is a text predictor, not an assistant. Two further stages shape behavior:
Fine-tuning: continue training on curated examples: your domain’s documents, or demonstrations of helpful question-answering
Alignment (RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback): humans rank the model’s answers; RL: the same reward-driven learning from Class 3’s Grid World and Pac-Man: nudges the model toward answers people prefer
These make a base model more helpful, safe, or specialized: but they do not make it omniscient. Tuning shapes how it answers, not what is true
Note
Class 5 opens with exactly this journey: base model → assistant: including what alignment costs, what it fixes, and the strange failure modes it leaves behind.

chunks.title: GPT: Predict the Next Word, at Scale
chunks.passage:
GPT: Predict the Next Word, at Scale
GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) has one training objective: predict the next token.
Given “The cat sat on the,” predict “mat.” That’s it: billions of times, on billions of documents.
From this simple objective, the model learns grammar, facts, reasoning, and coding: all as a side effect of getting better at prediction.
Note
GPT-1 (2018) had 117 million parameters. GPT-5 (2025) has an estimated 5 trillion. Same idea, 40,000x bigger: and the results went from “interesting toy” to “writes better than most humans.”

chunks.title: Beyond Text: The Same Machine, More Senses
chunks.passage:
Beyond Text: The Same Machine, More Senses
Multimodal means working with more than one kind of data. Different inputs become vectors: lists of numbers that attention can combine.
[Image description] Four inputs feed one multimodal model. A text question, What is the dog doing?, becomes word tokens; an image of a running dog is divided into patches; audio is split into short frames; and video contains frames across time. Each input is encoded as numerical vectors. Attention connects their representations inside the model, which generates the response, The dog is running, with possible spoken output.
Same attention idea, different input encoders. Supported inputs and outputs depend on the model; numbers are illustrative.
Why it matters: Ask a question about a screenshot, discuss a recording, or describe an image to generate. Context limits, hallucinations, and processing costs still matter.

Slide 2 of 2: LLMs Are Probabilistic
The model does not produce one guaranteed answer.
It produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens, then samples from it.
same prompt can produce different answers
better prompts reshape the distribution
more context changes what becomes likely

chunks.title: “It Knows” Is a Risky Shorthand
chunks.passage:
“It Knows” Is a Risky Shorthand
An LLM contains learned statistical structure in its parameters. It does not consult a verified, current, cited database unless you give it one.
That single sentence explains most of what this class covers:
why prompting works — you’re reshaping which continuation is likely
why hallucination happens — plausible ≠ verified
why RAG exists — to bolt a real, cited knowledge source onto the statistical machine

chunks.title: The Probability Distribution Is the Steering Surface
chunks.passage:
The Probability Distribution Is the Steering Surface
[Image description] Two complete inputs feed the same unchanged language model. Left input: The cat sat on the. Right input: The room has a soft rug, followed by The cat sat on the, both inside one input box. Arrows connect each input to the model and then its next-token probabilities. With added context, illustrative probabilities shift from mat 60%, rug 25%, floor 10%, other 5% to mat 15%, rug 70%, floor 10%, other 5%. Different input leads to different probabilities; it does not guarantee a particular token.

Why prompting matters: prompts steer the probability distribution
Why exact tasks need code: probabilities are not enough for precise pipelines
Why context matters: the model only sees what you put in the window

chunks.passage:
Temperature: The Creativity Dial
Every API call includes a temperature setting — a number that controls how “random” the output is.
|
Low temp |
High temp |
Good for |

Risk |

Note
Temperature changes variety, not intelligence. Lower temperature favors more likely continuations; higher temperature explores more possibilities and raises variance. It doesn’t make the model smarter or dumber — it changes how adventurous the sampling is.

chunks.title: What Is Fine-Tuning?
chunks.passage: What Is Fine-Tuning?

chunks.title: Fine-Tuning Reshapes the Distribution
chunks.passage:
Fine-Tuning Reshapes the Distribution
In Class 4 we saw you can take a pretrained model and fine-tune it — train it further on specific data.
But what does that actually mean? It shifts which tokens the model considers likely.
Same prompt, completely different predictions — because the weights changed.
Note
Fine-tuning is expensive and permanent — it changes the model’s weights. Prompting is cheap and temporary — it steers the same frozen model. Most of this class is about prompting, because that’s what you’ll use day-to-day.

chunks.title: RLHF — How Models Learn to Be Helpful
chunks.passage:
RLHF — How Models Learn to Be Helpful
Fine-tuning on examples makes a model follow instructions. But how does it learn to be helpful, polite, safe? Not from raw internet. From humans.
Post-training is three stages — and each one uses a learning paradigm from Classes 3 and 4:
Pretraining (unsupervised) — predict next token from raw internet. No labels — just patterns in text. Knows everything, does nothing useful.
SFT — Supervised Fine-Tuning (supervised) — labeled instruction → good-response pairs. This is what most people call “fine-tuning.”
RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (reinforcement) — remember Pac-Man from Class 3? Same loop: try an action, get a reward, learn. Only now the “reward” is human preference (A vs. B, which is better?), encoded in a reward model and optimized via PPO or DPO.
Tip
Callback to Classes 3 and 4. The same three learning paradigms you met earlier — unsupervised, supervised, reinforcement — are literally the three stages of training a modern LLM. In order.
Important
MBA lens. A prompt can’t override what RLHF taught. That’s the difference between personality (prompt-level, changeable per-session) and values (weight-level, baked in forever). Firms pick an RLHF recipe the same way they pick a hiring rubric — it determines who the model becomes.
(In Class 7 we’ll see why Anthropic, OpenAI, and Character.AI all hire philosophers for this step.)

chunks.title: …But It’s Super Expensive
chunks.passage:
…But It’s Super Expensive
Training: GPT-4 ~$100M · frontier runs cross $1B by 2027
Inference: ~0.3 Wh per ChatGPT query · billions of queries/day
You spend all that on one specific model — and a better one drops 6 months later.
So instead of changing the model… we just talk to it better. That’s what prompting is.

chunks.title: Three Levers, Three Jobs
chunks.passage:
Three Levers, Three Jobs
[Image description] Three distinct mechanisms. Prompting: Compare, then verify selects a blue reasoning path through Compare, Check, and Answer among gray alternatives, without changing model weights. Retrieval: a highlighted passage from external documents crosses a dashed model boundary into context and informs the answer, without changing weights. Fine-tuning: before and after maps show the same six embedding points moving from mixed positions into two groups after training updates the weights. The paths and embedding maps are conceptual illustrations.
The first two change the request. Fine-tuning changes the model.

chunks.title: Prompting
chunks.passage: Prompting

chunks.title: Prompting Is Probability Steering
chunks.passage:
Prompting Is Probability Steering
Prompting is not magic. It is guidance.
When you add detail, examples, constraints, and formatting requirements, you are shrinking the space of acceptable continuations and making the “right” answer more likely.
Theoretical Reason Specific Prompts Work
Specific prompts reduce ambiguity. Less ambiguity means lower entropy in the next-token distribution, so the model is less likely to wander into the wrong answer shape.

chunks.title: Don’t Mistake the Mask for the Model
chunks.passage:
Don’t Mistake the Mask for the Model
Important
Whatever polite, helpful voice comes out of the API — underneath is a next-token predictor trained on the internet, shaped by RLHF into something that sounds human. Prompt it like a tool, not a colleague. You’ll design better.

chunks.title: Attention Failure — The Model Answers the Wrong Question
chunks.passage:
Attention Failure — The Model Answers the Wrong Question
Same prompt, two tries. The first misses the intent entirely — only a follow-up aligns it.
Important
The model isn’t stupid — it’s under-specified. Attention latched onto “should I drive or walk” (a distance question) and ignored that the car is the whole point. This is the everyday failure mode prompting exists to fix.

chunks.title: Why Voice-to-Text Prompts Can Help
chunks.passage:
Why Voice-to-Text Prompts Can Help
Many people get better results when they talk to the model instead of typing a short command.
Why?
speech naturally includes more context
people say the edge cases they would have omitted
they explain intent, not just task labels
longer natural prompts often reduce ambiguity
How to do it
WhisperFlow — free app, transcribes anywhere you can type (works system-wide)
Mac dictation — press 🎤 on the keyboard or double-tap Fn
Claude / ChatGPT voice — tap the mic icon in the app to speak your prompt directly
Dictate the messy version first. Then tighten it into bullets, constraints, examples, and output format.

chunks.title: LLMs Do Not Start Fresh Per Message
chunks.passage:
LLMs Do Not Start Fresh Per Message
Each new request brings the conversation so far back to the model.
Simplified chat: earlier messages are included again. Long conversations may be trimmed or summarized.

chunks.title: Context Is Everything
chunks.passage:
Context Is Everything
[Image description] The same message, Meet me by the bank, points to two different scenes. On the left, the earlier chat says Let's watch the ducks, and two people meet on a grassy riverbank beside ducks and a river. On the right, the earlier chat says I need to deposit a check, and two people meet outside a financial bank branch. The earlier conversation changes the intended meaning of bank.
Same words. Different context. Different meaning.

chunks.title: Your Prompt Is Context
chunks.passage:
Your Prompt Is Context
The words you type or say become part of what the model uses to answer.
[Image description] Two spoken prompts. Little context: Help me prepare. Useful context: I present tomorrow. My audience is MBA students. I have five minutes. Help me prepare. The request stays the same while background details are added.
More relevant context gives the model less to guess.

chunks.title: Rambling Is a Fine First Draft
chunks.passage:
Rambling Is a Fine First Draft
Use voice mode or dictation. You do not need polished prose.
[Image description] A rambling spoken request mentions a presentation tomorrow, MBA students who have not studied AI, a five-minute limit, and help choosing what to cover. Colored annotations identify the audience, constraint and ask within the ordinary speech.
Attention helps connect details across the message, even out of order.
We often skip details when typing. Speaking can help us include them.

chunks.title: End With a Clear Ask
chunks.passage:
End With a Clear Ask
Tell it the situation, then the work you want done.
Situation
I’m presenting AI to MBA students tomorrow.
What matters
They are beginners. I have five minutes. I want them to understand attention.
Clear ask
Suggest a three-point outline and one everyday analogy. Avoid equations.
Context tells it what matters. The ask tells it what to do.

chunks.title: Give the Details That Change the Answer
chunks.passage:
Give the Details That Change the Answer
Before sending, check four things:
Who and why
Name the audience and what you want to achieve.
Useful background
Include the facts, examples, or text it needs.
Constraints
Say what must fit: time, budget, tone, or length.
Deliverable
Ask for an outline, comparison, draft, or recommendation.
If a detail would change your answer, include it.

chunks.title: Try It: Speak the Context, Then Ask
chunks.passage:
Try It: Speak the Context, Then Ask
60 seconds · Pick something you actually need help with.
1 · Talk for 30 seconds.
Explain the situation, what matters, and what makes it difficult.
2 · Finish with “What I need from you is…”
Name one clear deliverable.
3 · Read the answer.
Did it use your context? Correct anything it misunderstood.
Keep the useful detail. Make the ask unmistakable.

chunks.title: What Is a Context Window?
chunks.passage:
What Is a Context Window?
The maximum the model can hold at once. Your messages and its replies share that space.
Context window12 / 160 tokens · 8%
InstructionsYour messagesLLM repliesSpace left
A new chat. Instructions already take up some space.
Watch both sides of the conversation fill the same window.
Tiny demo window · illustrative token counts · earlier messages stay in context

chunks.title: How Big Is a Context Window?
chunks.passage:
How Big Is a Context Window?
State-of-the-art models like Claude Opus have a context window of 1 million tokens.
[Image description] The three books of the Lord of the Rings trilogy.
[Image description] User-provided screenshot showing a context window 52% full, with 136k of 258k tokens used.
[Image description] User-provided screenshot showing context usage of 185.4k out of 1 million tokens, or 19%, above a separate plan usage panel.
How much is that? The entire Lord of the Rings trilogy, all three books, is roughly 500,000 tokens.
A 1M-token context window can hold two copies of the full trilogy and still have room left.
More context = you can feed entire codebases, full documents, or long conversation histories, and the model reasons over all of it at once.

chunks.title: Bigger Context Is Not a Free Solution
chunks.passage:
Bigger Context Is Not a Free Solution
It raises cost and latency, can bury important evidence, and still requires selecting what should matter now.
Cost — you pay for every token, every turn (the window gets resent)
Latency — more tokens to read = slower first response
Attention — a needle in a 900K-token haystack is still a needle
The model only sees the active context — it has no durable memory of your previous chat unless a system deliberately sends relevant information again. A bigger window changes how much you can send, not whether you have to choose.

chunks.title: Context Rot Is Real
chunks.passage:
Context Rot Is Real
As prompts become cluttered, a model can miss, misweight, or contradict material already present. More text can make an answer worse.
[Image description] A long transcript contains an old $10k budget near the start, a $15k update in the middle, and other discussion. Tangled amber and gray paths converge on an LLM, while the update has a faint dashed teal path. Asked for the current budget, the model answers $10k, using the old plan even though the correct update is present. The paths illustrate a possible failure, not measured attention weights.
When a long chat gets confused, start a new chat and bring only what matters.

chunks.title: But Context Fills Up — Enter Compression
chunks.passage:
But Context Fills Up — Enter Compression
Even 1M tokens isn’t infinite. When the window fills, compaction summarizes old conversation into a compact block, freeing up space to keep going.
Compaction is lossy summarization — it preserves some decisions and discards detail. Design what gets retained rather than hoping the model remembers correctly.
Note
In Claude Code, /compact triggers this manually — it also happens automatically around 95% usage. Anything that must persist should live in CLAUDE.md or a plan file: compaction doesn’t touch those.

chunks.title: Put Stable Rules in Stable Places
chunks.passage:
Put Stable Rules in Stable Places
System instructions, durable project files, and structured state are better homes for rules than a long casual conversation.
Where it lives |
Survives compaction? |
Survives a new chat? |
Chat message from 40 turns ago |
❌ maybe, as a summary |
❌ |
System prompt |
✅ |
✅ (if the app resends it) |
CLAUDE.md / project file |
✅ |
✅ |
A file on disk the model can re-read |
✅ |
✅ |
This table is the whole memory strategy: conversation is volatile, files are durable. It’s also the design principle behind your personal wiki assignment.

chunks.title: Why Everyone Talks About Tokens
chunks.passage:
Why Everyone Talks About Tokens
Each token the model processes is a pass through a neural network with trillions of parameters, running on GPUs. That’s expensive compute — and it’s why everything AI is priced per token.
Important
Input is cheap, output is expensive. Input tokens are read in parallel (one pass). Output tokens are generated one-by-one, each requiring its own pass. That’s why generating a long answer costs more than reading a long document.
Tokens are the unit of work: models see token pieces, not exactly words — and tokens determine context use, latency, and price. When Class 6 turns to cost engineering, this slide is the foundation.

chunks.title: Prompt Engineering
chunks.passage: Prompt Engineering

chunks.title: .md Files — Why They’re Everywhere in AI
chunks.passage:
.md Files — Why They’re Everywhere in AI
A .md file is a markdown file — a simple way to write formatted text using plain characters. No special software — just a text file.
You write this:
# Meeting Notes
## Action Items
Today we discussed **two options**:
- Option A: launch in *June*
- Option B: wait for Q3
> Decision: go with Option A
It renders as this:
Meeting Notes
Action Items
Today we discussed two options:
Option A: launch in June
Option B: wait for Q3
Decision: go with Option A
# = title, ## = subtitle, **bold**, *italic*, - = bullet. That’s most of what you need.
Markdown is everywhere — these slides, Notion, GitHub, and apps like Obsidian all use it. It’s also the most popular format for writing AI instructions and knowledge bases because it’s structured enough for machines to parse but readable enough for humans to write.

chunks.title: What Is a System Prompt?
chunks.passage:
What Is a System Prompt?
Every AI app has secret instructions the user never sees — written by the developer before you ever type anything. Think of it like a job briefing before an employee’s first day.
# ROLE
You are a PM interview coach for MBA students.
# PERSONALITY
Supportive but direct. Use frameworks like STAR.
Never be condescending. Keep answers under 200 words.
# BOUNDARIES
- Only help with PM interviews
- No salary negotiation or offer advice
- If asked about other roles, say “I specialize in PM interviews”
# OUTPUT RULES
- Always use STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
- End with one follow-up question to improve the answer
—
USER: {{user_message}}
← Role — who the model is
← Personality — tone and style
← Boundaries — what it refuses
← Output rules — format of every response
← Your message gets injected here
This entire string is sent to the LLM every time you send a message. The user only types the yellow part — everything above it is invisible to them.
Important
Remember how fine-tuning costs millions and goes obsolete in 6 months? A system prompt does much of the same job — reshaping behavior — but it’s free, instant, and easy to change. That’s why most products start here.

chunks.title: CLAUDE.md & Project Files
chunks.passage:
CLAUDE.md & Project Files
Markdown is just a simple way to write formatted text — headings, bullet points, bold — using plain characters you already know. No special software needed.
A CLAUDE.md file is a small document that lives inside your project folder. It tells the AI things like:
“Our brand voice is warm and professional — never sarcastic”
“When writing emails, always include a clear subject line and sign off with the team name”
“Budgets are in USD. Fiscal year starts in April”
Tools like Claude Code read this file automatically and inject it into every conversation — like giving the AI a cheat sheet about your team before it starts working.
You write it once. It applies to every conversation in that project. No copy-pasting context every time.

chunks.title: What Gets Sent Each Turn
chunks.passage:
What Gets Sent Each Turn
The model reads all of this fresh every turn — no memory between calls
Long chats cost more because the input keeps growing
Old context can distract — sometimes “start a new chat” is the right fix
Good early framing (system prompt) helps the entire conversation

chunks.title: The Golden Rule of Prompting
chunks.passage:
The Golden Rule of Prompting
A good prompt has five parts — most people only give one.
Tip
You don’t need all five every time — but the more you give, the less the model has to guess.

Your check: have a conversation. Change only the agent instructions in AGENTS.md to a friendly personality, restart, and ask the same question.

chunks.title: Thinking Models
chunks.passage: Thinking Models

chunks.title: The Biggest Shift Since GPT
chunks.passage:
The Biggest Shift Since GPT
Until September 2024, every LLM worked the same way: you ask, it immediately starts talking. No pause, no reflection — just next-token prediction as fast as possible.
Then OpenAI released o1 — a model that stops and thinks before answering. It scored in the 89th percentile on competitive programming and placed among the top 500 US math olympiad students.
The trick? “Think step by step” used to be something you wrote in the prompt. Now it’s trained into the model itself.

chunks.title: What Are “Thinking” Models?
chunks.passage:
What Are “Thinking” Models?
Most models answer immediately — you ask, they respond.
Thinking models (Claude with extended thinking, OpenAI o-series) pause and reason before answering.
What happens during the “thinking” phase?
The model generates an internal chain of reasoning — you can often see it
It breaks the problem down into smaller pieces
It considers different approaches
It checks its own logic before committing to an answer
Remember: more relevant context = better answer. Thinking models create their own extra context before responding.

chunks.title: Same Puzzle, Thinking On — Intent Catches Itself
chunks.passage:
Same Puzzle, Thinking On — Intent Catches Itself
Same prompt. Thinking mode on.
The model previews its own reasoning (“Oh, I see the catch here…”) before committing.
It catches the intent — the car has to get to the wash — with no user correction.
Tip
Earlier we needed a second message to fix attention. Here, the second “message” happens inside the model’s own head. That’s the whole pitch for thinking models.

chunks.title: Thinking Is Not a Permission Slip to Skip Evaluation
chunks.passage:
Thinking Is Not a Permission Slip to Skip Evaluation
A more capable model can still use the wrong data, misunderstand the goal, or confidently produce an unverifiable claim.
Thinking mode raises the floor on hard reasoning tasks. It does not grant the model access to facts it never saw, and it does not make outputs deterministic. Everything we said about probability distributions still applies — the distribution just got reshaped by better internal context.

chunks.title: Tip: Use Plan Mode
chunks.passage:
Tip: Use Plan Mode
Thinking models reason automatically. But you can also force this behavior — that’s what plan mode does.
Tools like Claude Code (/plan), Codex, and Gemini CLI let you ask the AI to plan before executing.
You say:
“Build me an interview prep app”
→
Plan mode generates:
Goal: Web app for PM interview prep
Stack: Next.js + Claude API
Features:
1. Role selector (APM, PM, GPM)
2. Question generator by category
3. Answer evaluator with rubric
UI: Single page, chat-style
Constraints: No auth, no DB
Try voice mode — explain what you want out loud. The AI turns your rambling into a structured plan, which gives it dramatically better context to work from.
Two things make plan mode powerful:
It forces longer thinking — the model spends more time reasoning before writing any code
It saves the plan to a file — so the blueprint lives outside the context window. Even in a long session where early messages get forgotten, the plan file stays. The model can always look back at it.
Tip
Prompting is asking for a building. Plan mode is asking for the blueprint first — and pinning it to the wall so nobody forgets it.

chunks.title: Model Tiers
chunks.passage:
Model Tiers
CHOOSING A MODEL 1 / 3 · TIERS & SIZE
The learned weights from Class 4 are parameters. B = billion parameters.
[Image description] Four conceptual two-dimensional neural networks illustrate relative product tiers. Efficient: GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku. Balanced: GPT-5.6 Terra and Claude Sonnet. Advanced: GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5. Frontier: GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1. These pairings are teaching comparisons, not measured equivalences or known parameter-size classes. Actual parameter counts are undisclosed.
Relative product tiers, not measured size classes. Networks are illustrative; paired models are not necessarily equivalent.
Parameter counts: undisclosed
No defensible estimates for these models. Price, speed and capability do not reveal the number of weights.
For scale: published open weights
Qwen3 comes in 1.7B, 8B and 32B, plus a 235B-total / 22B-active mixture of experts.
Choose by results on your task, then compare speed and cost.

chunks.title: Reasoning Effort: Low to Max
chunks.passage:
Reasoning Effort: Low to Max
CHOOSING A MODEL 2 / 3 · EFFORT
Reasoning tokens are pieces of intermediate working, used to plan, compare or check.
[Image description] Prompt and reasoning generated so far enter the same neural network, whose weights stay fixed. A conceptual Keep reasoning decision branches toward a visible answer or another reasoning token. Continuing appends that token to the sequence and repeats the loop. A dashed arrow shows higher effort encouraging more reasoning. Below, low effort has a shorter illustrative sequence than higher effort, both ending in a visible answer. The decision is a teaching abstraction, not a separate checker or a guaranteed verification step.
LOW
Routine extraction
and simple edits
MEDIUM
Compare options
and plan a task
HIGH
Many constraints
or a difficult bug
XHIGH
Explore several
hard approaches
MAX
Hardest problems;
time is secondary
More reasoning usually costs more time and tokens. It does not guarantee a better answer.
Conceptual decision, not a separate checker. Counts are illustrative; a reasoning step can use many tokens. Levels vary by model.

chunks.title: Open Models & Running Locally
chunks.passage:
Open Models & Running Locally
[Image description] Three-part whiteboard infographic. 1: Qwen or Gemma illustrated by connected nodes with numerical weights. Open weights means downloadable, inspectable model parameters; code and training data may be unavailable. Open source AI also includes code, enough training-data information, and freedoms to use, study, modify and share the system. Check each release's license. 2: Prompts and files flow through a local model to an answer within your machine. Fully local tools and logging can keep data on-device. 3: Running needs RAM or VRAM for weights, context and runtime, with spare room. Raw 16-bit versus 4-bit weight memory: 8B, 16 versus 4 GB; 32B, 64 versus 16 GB; 70B, 140 versus 35 GB. Quantization can change quality. Apple Silicon shares RAM with the OS.

chunks.title: Hallucination Is a System Property
chunks.passage: Hallucination Is a System Property

chunks.title: Why Fluent Systems Can Be Wrong
chunks.passage:
Why Fluent Systems Can Be Wrong
The next-token objective rewards plausible continuation. It does not guarantee source access, truth verification, or current information.
Fluent does not mean factual. A convincing answer can still be unsupported.
Probability is not truth. The chart scores possible next tokens, not whether the claim is correct.
Plausibility without evidence is the failure mode. Ground the answer in evidence you can check.
[Image description] Whiteboard diagram of next-token selection. The prompt Our revenue was $ leads to an illustrative probability distribution: 12 at 55 percent, 8 at 25 percent, 15 at 15 percent, and other tokens at 5 percent. The token 15 is sampled this time despite having a lower probability than 12, then appended to the prompt. Generation repeats with the updated context. No source has been checked: likely next token does not mean verified fact.
Treat hallucination as a system property to manage. The architecture around the model is something you control.

chunks.title: Four Defenses
chunks.passage:
Four Defenses
[Image description] Four whiteboard illustrations: 1. RAG, a retrieved document passage feeds a model and its answer. 2. Citing sources, a citation links an answer to its supporting passage. 3. Higher thinking modes, an effort slider increases reasoning work on a scratchpad. 4. Lower temperatures where supported, a dial reduces sampling randomness and concentrates probability on the same leading token.

chunks.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
chunks.passage: Retrieval Augmented Generation

chunks.title: There’s Still a Problem
chunks.passage:
There’s Still a Problem
We’ve covered prompts, context, and thinking — but all of it only lasts for one conversation. Start a new chat tomorrow, and the model has no idea who you are, what your project is, or what you talked about.
Even the smartest LLM has the memory of Dory from Finding Nemo — brilliant in the moment, completely blank the next.

chunks.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
chunks.passage:
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
An LLM only knows what was in its training data. Try asking Claude “who won the Super Bowl last month?” — it can’t answer. Its knowledge is frozen at the date it was trained.
Same thing if you ask about your company’s latest earnings, a new HR policy, or what happened in the news yesterday. The model has never seen any of it.
You could paste everything into the chat each time — but that doesn’t scale. Imagine copy-pasting 50 pages of company docs every conversation.
RAG = Retrieval Augmented Generation

chunks.title: You Already Use RAG
chunks.passage:
You Already Use RAG
When ChatGPT searches the web before answering — that’s RAG
When Claude Code reads your project files before writing code — that’s RAG
When a company chatbot answers from internal HR docs — that’s RAG
When a customer support tool pulls answers from your help center — that’s RAG
Note
86% of enterprises use RAG to connect AI to their own data. — Databricks, 2025

chunks.title: Why RAG Matters
chunks.passage:
Why RAG Matters
1. Grounds answers in evidence → fewer hallucinations
The model answers from retrieved documents, not from memory. If the document says revenue was $12.5M, that’s what gets cited — not a guess.
2. Uses private knowledge without retraining
Your company’s internal docs, your database, yesterday’s news — just retrieve and inject into the prompt. No fine-tuning, no $100K training run, no model that goes stale in 6 months.
This is why businesses love RAG: plug in your own data, keep using the same model.

chunks.title: How RAG Works
chunks.passage:
How RAG Works
Find the relevant information, then give it to the AI with the question.
A question starts the search.
Illustrative animation, not a live AI call. Retrieval adds context; it does not retrain the model.

chunks.title: Chunking Text
chunks.passage:
Chunking Text
Chunking splits a long document into smaller, useful passages.
Keep one idea and its context together.
Retrieve the pieces that fit the question.
Give those pieces to the AI as context.
[Image description] Whiteboard illustration: a long document with three colored sections is split at section boundaries into three chunks. A question selects one relevant chunk, which enters the AI's context. Keep related ideas together.

chunks.title: Vector Databases & Vector Search
chunks.passage:
Vector Databases & Vector Search
A vector database stores numerical representations of your text, called embeddings.
Similar meanings sit close together.
Vector search finds chunks near the question.
The AI reads those chunks to answer.
[Image description] Whiteboard meaning map inside a vector database. Saved document chunks form travel, food, and finance clusters. The question Where can I stay lands near travel chunks, including Hotels. Vector search selects nearby chunks and returns their text. Similar meanings sit close together.

chunks.title: AI Can Write SQL
chunks.passage:
AI Can Write SQL
AI can turn a question into SQL, the language used to query a database.
The AI writes the query.
Your app runs it with permitted access.
The AI uses the returned data to answer.
[Image description] Whiteboard flow: a user asks How many customers? The AI writes SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers; as its output. The app runs this SQL against the database. The database returns a count of 128, which goes back to the AI. The AI explains: You have 128 customers. The AI writes the query; the database supplies the facts.
